notes.b: Almost every rule for handling food comes from two facts about food poisoning bacteria: they multiply fastest in warm food, and they travel easily from one food to another. Knowing these makes the individual rules easy to remember.
points: Food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest in the danger zone, 5°C to 63°C. This is why safe preparation keeps food cold, hot, or moving quickly through that range.

Cross-contamination is the transfer of bacteria from raw food to cooked or ready-to-eat food, directly or by hands, chopping boards, cloths, utensils or meat juices. This is why raw and cooked foods are kept apart.
Freezing does not kill bacteria, it only stops them multiplying, and thawing lets them start multiplying again. So frozen food must be handled with care once it thaws.
notes.tip: In discuss questions on storage, cooking and reheating, give the temperature or rule and the reason it prevents food poisoning. Cooking at 50°C does not kill all bacteria, so that statement is false, and moving bacteria from raw to cooked food is cross-contamination.

notes.b: Storage aims to keep food cold or frozen so bacteria cannot multiply, and to stop bacteria passing from one food to another. Short questions usually ask for three to six storage guidelines.
points: Cover all food and store it in sealed containers, which prevents drying out, odour transfer and cross-contamination.
Keep perishable food (food that spoils quickly) in the fridge at 5°C or below, which slows the growth of bacteria. Check the fridge and freezer temperature with a thermometer.
Store raw meat, poultry and fish on the lowest shelf, on a plate and loosely covered with the shop wrapping removed, so that juices cannot drip onto cooked or ready-to-eat food.
Keep raw and cooked foods apart, covered or in sealed containers, so bacteria cannot pass between them.
Cool cooked food quickly before refrigerating or freezing it, and do not overpack the fridge, so that cold air can circulate around the food.
Check the use-by or best-before date of each food and follow the storage instructions on its label. Use-by is a safety date for highly perishable food, while best-before is a quality date.
Remove fruit and vegetables from plastic wrapping, which encourages mould, and check them regularly for mould.
Store dry foods in a cool, dry, well-ventilated cupboard, in vermin-proof containers, and keep storage areas clean.
Keep perishable food out of the fridge for the shortest possible time while it is being prepared, because food left in warm air soon enters the danger zone.
notes.tip: To store raw meat safely, say lowest shelf, on a plate, loosely covered, so juices cannot drip onto cooked food. Use-by and best-before are different: one is about safety and the other about quality.

notes.b: Freezing keeps food safe for a long time, but only if it is frozen and thawed properly. Bacteria are not killed by freezing, so the care taken when thawing matters.
points: Freeze food quickly at −25°C, then store it at −18°C.
Defrost frozen food completely before cooking, preferably in the fridge on the bottom shelf, so that it thaws slowly and any drips cannot reach other food.
Never refreeze food that has thawed, because bacteria multiply while it thaws.
notes.tip: Give both freezer figures when asked: fast-freeze at −25°C, store at −18°C. State the rule as never refreeze thawed food.

notes.b: Cooking and reheating must heat food right through to kill bacteria, and hot food must then stay hot or be eaten promptly. Otherwise bacteria multiply again in the danger zone.
points: Cook food thoroughly, using the right time and temperature, and turn or stir it so that heat reaches the centre. Cook meat, poultry and minced meat right through, to a core temperature of at least 72°C for poultry.
Reheat food quickly until it is above 100°C throughout, and reheat it only once.
High-risk foods such as stews and gravies should be brought to boiling when reheated, because their moist, protein-rich nature suits bacteria.
Cover food when reheating. In a microwave, stir or turn the food and allow standing time, so that heat reaches all parts evenly, and follow the appliance's instructions.
Serve cooked food immediately. If holding it hot, keep it above 63°C, because bacteria multiply rapidly between 5°C and 63°C.
Eat food that has been held hot within about 90 minutes (1.5 hours).
Do not keep food in the danger zone. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate them and use them soon.
notes.tip: Use the figures that the marking schemes use: reheat above 100°C throughout and only once, poultry at least 72°C at the core, and hot holding above 63°C. Always add the reason, which is that bacteria multiply between 5°C and 63°C.

notes.b: People carry food poisoning bacteria on their hands, hair, skin and clothes, so the person preparing food is a major source of contamination. Examiners usually ask for four to six personal hygiene points.
points: Wash hands in hot water with liquid soap, and a nailbrush for the nails, before handling food, because hands carry food poisoning bacteria. Dry them on a clean towel or paper towel.
Wash hands after the toilet, sneezing or coughing, changing nappies, handling pets, handling rubbish and handling raw meat.
Keep nails short and clean and remove jewellery before preparing food, because dirt and bacteria collect under nails and around jewellery.
Tie hair back or cover it. Wear a clean apron or clothing, and change it if it becomes soiled.
Cover cuts, boils and sores with a brightly coloured waterproof plaster, so that infection cannot pass to food and the plaster can be seen if it falls into the food.
Do not cough or sneeze over food, and do not taste food with your fingers or lick your fingers.
Do not prepare or serve food for others while suffering from diarrhoea or vomiting, because the illness can pass to the people eating it.
notes.tip: Say a brightly coloured plaster, and give the reason, so it can be seen if it falls in food. For hand washing, name hot water, liquid soap and a nailbrush.

notes.b: A clean kitchen with sensible habits stops bacteria building up on surfaces and equipment and passing to food. Four kitchen hygiene practices is a common exam question.
points: Clean and disinfect work surfaces often, and wash equipment in hot water and detergent. Clean as you go.
Use colour-coded chopping boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked foods, to prevent cross-contamination.
Never prepare raw and cooked foods on the same surface.
Handle food as little as possible during preparation, and keep it covered, because every touch can pass on bacteria.
Floors, walls and work surfaces should be easy to clean, and the kitchen should have good lighting.
Effective ventilation reduces condensation, which encourages the growth of micro-organisms.
The kitchen should have a clean water supply and no access for pets or pests.
Keep a covered waste bin and empty it regularly, and change clean cloths and dishtowels often.
notes.tip: For food hygiene as a heading, include cooking thoroughly, thawing fully, and buying from reputable shops after checking dates and packaging. Give a reason with each point, such as colour-coded boards preventing cross-contamination.

keyTerms.definition: The transfer of bacteria from raw food, or from unclean hands and surfaces, to cooked or ready-to-eat food.
The temperature range of 5°C to 63°C in which bacteria multiply rapidly in food.
Keeping cooked food above 63°C until it is served, so that bacteria do not multiply.
Freezing food quickly at a very low temperature, such as −25°C, so that only small ice crystals form.
Thawing frozen food completely before cooking it, preferably in the fridge.
Heating previously cooked food until it is above 100°C throughout, and only once.
The habits of a food handler, such as handwashing, clean clothing and covering cuts, that stop micro-organisms reaching food.
Keeping the kitchen, its surfaces, equipment and water supply clean so that food is not contaminated.

factCards.term: Three storage temperatures for home food
factCards.definition: Below 5°C in the fridge, −18°C for frozen storage, and −25°C for fast-freezing.

factCards.term: Two temperatures for safe reheating and hot holding
factCards.definition: Reheat to above 100°C throughout, and hold cooked food above 63°C.

factCards.term: Five occasions when hands must be washed
factCards.definition: After sneezing or coughing, after using the toilet, after changing nappies, after handling pets, and after handling rubbish.

factCards.term: Three measures against cross-contamination in the kitchen
factCards.definition: Colour-coded chopping boards, separate utensils for raw and cooked meat, and no shared surfaces for raw and cooked food.

factCards.term: Range in which bacteria multiply rapidly in food
Reason for storing raw meat below cooked food
factCards.definition: So that juices dripping from the raw meat cannot contaminate cooked or ready-to-eat food.

factCards.term: Maximum time for hot food held above 63°C
factCards.definition: About 90 minutes, after which the food should not be eaten.

questions.prompt: Outline two guidelines for storing perishable food safely in a home fridge, giving a reason for each.
questions.model: Keep the fridge below 5°C, which slows the growth of bacteria in perishable food. Cover all food, so that it does not dry out or pick up odours and cannot contaminate other food. Store raw meat on the lowest shelf, covered, below cooked food, so that juices cannot drip onto cooked food. Do not overpack the fridge, so that cold air circulates around the food. Cool cooked food before refrigerating it.

questions.prompt: Discuss the personal hygiene and kitchen hygiene practices that prevent food from being contaminated during preparation and cooking.
questions.model: Personal hygiene: wash hands in hot water with liquid soap and a nailbrush before handling food and after sneezing, coughing, using the toilet, changing nappies, handling pets or rubbish; keep nails short and clean and remove jewellery; wear a clean apron; cover cuts with a brightly coloured plaster; do not prepare food while suffering from diarrhoea or vomiting; cough and sneeze away from food. Kitchen hygiene: clean and disinfect surfaces often and wash equipment in hot water and detergent; use colour-coded chopping boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked meat; do not prepare cooked and raw food on the same surface; handle food as little as possible; keep perishable food out of the fridge for the shortest time; keep the kitchen easy to clean, well lit and well ventilated to reduce condensation; provide a clean water supply and keep pets out of the kitchen.
